# Architecture notes

The Project Map shows runtime resources from `productview.yaml`: services, databases, storage and persistent CLI servers. Only connections between these resources are drawn. Specifications, test suites, one-off CLI tasks and issue sources remain in the YAML for their dedicated pages and traceability, but do not appear as runtime nodes. Roadmap items refer to component IDs where their work has an architectural effect. A real CLI can be added as a `commandTool` component; its `cli` metadata becomes a manpage-style manual under Run & Verify. This repository does not register a CLI merely to populate that page.

The Spec Kit adapter reads existing `.specify/` and `specs/<feature>/` artifacts without rewriting them. Optional `views.specifications.links` in `productview.yaml` connect feature or FR IDs to existing component and test IDs. The desktop compares those links with its current process state and recorded test events. It labels missing or stale evidence without claiming that file presence or completed checkboxes prove a release.

The current web prototype is a simulation. The desktop app can open a local repository, start configured services and command tools, run tests, read explicitly configured help output, and record activity in `.productview/`. Environment variable names are shared in YAML; values are encrypted in per-workspace macOS app data outside the repository and injected only into local commands started from the desktop app. OpenBuildRoom masks known values in command output and excludes the local store from MCP access. Live issue sync, telemetry and Railway deployment are planned integrations.

Build provenance is per executable component. Services and linked CLI tools can declare `build.file`, a repository-relative JSON artifact with `builtAt` (timezone-aware ISO 8601), `revision` and optional `version`. Without an explicit path, the desktop checks `build-info.json` and `dist/build-info.json` under that component's working directory. Only a build pipeline should write `builtAt`, after a successful build. The current Git HEAD is displayed as a separate source revision and cannot substitute for a build timestamp. On manual launch the main process snapshots the metadata and start time, records them in `.productview/events.jsonl`, and keeps the snapshot for the running process even if the file changes. The dashboard, map, Services and CLI Explorer render the same identity. MCP Explorer can read an explicitly declared build file for a local stdio server and separately shows the protocol-reported version and connection time. A remote MCP server has no local build timestamp unless its protocol supplies more data in the future. Missing metadata is reported as unavailable, not guessed from filesystem mtimes.

Product Chat can run the locally installed Codex CLI or Claude Code from the desktop app. Settings → AI & Chat stores the chosen provider and inspect/edit permission mode in app data, separate from the repository. Each request runs in the selected workspace with OpenBuildRoom's read-only MCP server and the agent's own configured tools. Chat prompts and replies are recorded in `.productview/events.jsonl`; local environment values are not included in the prompt or MCP output. The microphone uses macOS on-device speech recognition and inserts text into the composer before the user sends it.

Personal appearance and sidebar preferences stay local to the app or browser. Project connections are shared metadata in `productview.yaml`: GitHub uses `integration.repository`, Linear uses `integration.teamId`, and either may include a display `integration.url`. The Settings UI can edit these locations in a desktop workspace. It does not yet authenticate or fetch issues; credentials must not be committed to the repository.

The local backlog is repository-backed: each issue is a Markdown file in `product.backlogRoot` (default `backlog/`). Stable IDs and frontmatter carry workflow state; an optional `spec` path links an issue to a Spec Kit feature. The desktop app can create and edit these files without connecting an external tracker.

## MCP Explorer

## API Explorer

Project-local OpenAPI 3.x files are scanned read-only and listed beside HTTP APIs declared in `workspace.apiSources`. The file remains the source of truth for endpoint paths and summaries; the repository YAML stores only its relative path, a clean base URL and optional Bearer environment variable name. An API can be registered without a spec and tested with a manually entered relative path. The main process performs a request only after the user clicks Send, checks that the target stays on the selected origin, blocks redirects, applies a timeout and bounds the response preview. It resolves Bearer values from the local encrypted environment store and records only request metadata in Activity. Request headers, query values, body and response content are not persisted. The included Hello Workspace has a matching OpenAPI document for its real health and notes endpoints.

## MCP Explorer

The desktop main process uses the official MCP client SDK to connect to explicitly selected project servers over stdio, Streamable HTTP or legacy SSE. It keeps one client session per connected server, so several can remain connected while the user switches between them. Read-only discovery scans project-local MCP configuration and shared `workspace.mcpServers`; it does not launch anything. Add, link and remove actions update the YAML array atomically after schema validation; linked entries record the discovered source ID. The renderer gets safe server metadata, capabilities, schemas and user-requested results over IPC. Connect, disconnect and invocation metadata goes to `.productview/events.jsonl`; arguments and responses remain in memory. YAML declares only variable names; encrypted values are resolved in the main process when the user connects. The built-in OpenBuildRoom MCP server is the default example. OAuth login is outside this prototype.
